content.thinking:
I need to write the whole module without being able to typecheck it, so I'm planning carefully: a treasure hoard prop group in League of Legends style, with exaggerated dynamic shapes, saturated high-contrast accents, and glowing magic details readable from a top-down camera. Mostly plain objects, though a chest might need a lid hinge joint, and I'm checking the builder's requirement for exactly one root joint.

I'll create a root joint at the origin and a separate hinge joint for the lid, parenting the lid to root, with lid-related parts explicitly assigned to the lid bone and everything else defaulting to root to avoid relying on proximity-based joint assignment. I'll build a wrapper helper function that defaults to the root bone unless overridden, keeping things explicit and safe given I can't verify the API behavior interactively.

Now I'm planning the scene layout: a dragon's hoard with a coin mound roughly 2.2m across and 0.5m tall, a chest (~0.9×0.55×0.6m) sunk into the back of the mound, plus a crown, goblets, scattered gems, gold bars, and maybe a glowing crystal, pearls, a ring, or a scroll for flavor. I'm thinking the mound itself should be built from several overlapping flattened low-poly spheres rather than a symmetrical lathe shape, since a single lathe profile would look too uniform for a pile of coins.

For the coins, I'm budgeting triangle counts: an 8-sided cylinder comes to about 32 triangles each, so 500-600 coins merged by color category (gold, bright gold, silver, copper) stays well within a 60k triangle budget. I'll need to apply each coin's transform matrix before merging so they scatter naturally across the mound, using flat colors rather than painted textures for these merged batches.

For larger surfaces like the mound and chest, I'm leaning toward cel-style painted textures since the saturated look reads better at that scale, while keeping small objects on cheap flat colors — estimating texel density around 4mm which should be plenty sharp for a 6m² mound and 3m² chest.

For the coin pile itself, I'm wrapping a scale-pattern paint in a cel shader so it reads like overlapping coins with darker edges, then scattering actual coin geometry on top for stacks and loose pieces. For the mound's base shape I need hemispheres rather than full spheres, since a full sphere sunk at the equator would violate the floor-sinking constraint — so I'm building partial sphere geometries open at the bottom, sitting flush on the floor.

I'm arranging several overlapping hemispheres of varying radii and heights clustered around the origin to form an irregular mound silhouette, using flat faceted shading so the cel paint reads crisp two-tone facets. Then I'm figuring out the overall heap height so I can position a treasure chest tucked behind the mound at an appropriate scale.

I'm placing the chest off to the back-left, tilted and partially nestled into the coin pile, with its lid rotated open at roughly 105° to reveal gems inside — building the lid in its closed pose first so the hinge geometry stays correct, then posing it open afterward by rotating around the hinge axis.

Thinking about orientation, I'm weighing whether to keep the chest axis-aligned facing +Z for simplicity versus rotating it for a more dynamic composition, since any rotation complicates how I compute local coordinates for the lid's extra tilt.

I'll settle on axis-aligned placement at the back center, letting the hoard provide the asymmetry instead, and work out how the lid hinge joint should rotate about the x-axis when open.

Working through the rotation math to get the lid swinging upward correctly...

At 105° the lid leans back behind the chest with its interior facing the camera, showing the red velvet lining, and rises roughly 0.5 above the hinge for a total chest height near 0.9 — though I need to check whether it then overlaps the rear of the mound, since the chest's back sits around z=-0.55 and the lid extends backward from there.

I'm also double-checking the hinge joint setup: parts build in the closed pose, get their world transform set via the hinge object, then pose rotation applies afterward, which should work correctly for the handles. But I'm unsure about the default orientation of a joint with no aim direction — whether it just inherits the parent's orientation as identity, which matters for how the lid's rotation axis is actually defined in model space.

Now I'm working through the lid geometry itself, modeling it as a half-cylinder barrel-vault shape oriented along the X axis, with radius derived from the depth and hinged at the back edge, tracing through how the cylinder's sweep angle maps to the +Z/-Z positions.

Building the arch outline points manually to extrude a solid vaulted slab with flat end caps and a thin width, then planning to apply a wood grain paint texture...

Now I'm defining the strap orientation axes, then moving to the chest body itself: a box of walls (front, back, sides, bottom) left open at top, with a mounded coin heap hemisphere filling the interior above the rim.

I'm working out the chest's exact dimensions and position relative to the mound beneath it, checking how deep the body sinks into the terrain's hemisphere shape at that offset so the base sits naturally embedded.

I realize the mound currently buries the chest's front wall entirely, so I'm shifting the pile's center forward and reducing its radius so the front face stays partly visible, aiming for the classic look of coins spilling out in front of a mostly-exposed chest.

With that height worked out, I calculate the lock plate position to sit just above the coin line, then add side mounds flanking and behind the chest to bury its edges without hiding too much. Now I'm positioning the crown on the front-right slope of the pile, checking the local mound height there to set its resting tilt correctly.

Working out the crown geometry: a lathed headband ring with exaggerated proportions, topped by spikes arranged in a circle, tilted using an axis vector so it leans naturally into the mound rather than sitting perfectly upright.

I decide to build my own basis directly from the axis vector using cross products rather than trusting the ring item's tilt behavior, since I understand the math better. I'll also consider whether the lathe's axis option could help spin a cross-section around the tilted axis for the crown shape.

Now I'm designing the crown band's lathe profile, sketching out coordinates for the outer wall, top bevel, and inner wall to form a closed loop without self-crossing, aiming for a tall dynamic LoL-style crown with alternating points and a central glowing gem.

For the spires, I'm considering extruding flat blade-shaped outlines in the tangent plane along each point's radial axis, sketching an S-curve profile for a tall, elegant spire shape rather than simple cones.

Then I think about alternating tall and short spire heights with small ball tips, and placing eight small gem shapes along the band front, stretched octahedrons colored red, blue, and green.

I'm also planning gold beads along the band's top and bottom lip, plus a large glowing ruby centerpiece on a gold setting positioned toward the crown's front, computing the forward direction by projecting world-Z onto the local radial axis.

I'm adding small white pearl orbs to the spire tips, and shaping a domed red velvet cushion inside the crown using a lathe profile to simulate the interior lining visible from above.

Now I'm working out the crown's tilt direction so it leans naturally into the fallen pose, picking a tilt axis that angles the opening toward the camera so the front gem and interior cushion read clearly from the high 3/4 viewing angle.

Then I'm placing the crown at the (0.52, y, 0.62) mound, computing the mound height there (~0.265) and adjusting for the rim's slight tilt-induced drop so the crown base sits buried just enough into the gold surface, pruning out an extra mound I'd considered to keep the mound list clean.

For the gold bars, I'm working out how to fake trapezoidal ingot shapes using a 4-sided cylinder rotated 45° on the Y axis and non-uniformly scaled into a rectangular footprint, rather than boxes, so they read visually as stacked ingots with tapered sides.

I should bake the 45° rotation into the geometry itself with a one-time rotateY call, then scale along local axes and apply a separate yaw rotation per part for orientation. I'm also wondering if sharing that cached geometry across multiple meshes is safe, since mesh creation might mutate or bake transforms into it.

For safety I'll just use factory functions to generate fresh geometry each time rather than reuse references. Now I'm working out positions for a pile of ingots stacked at the left-front of the mound, computing the local mound height there to figure out how deep the bottom layer should sink in, settling on a base y around 0.16 with 0.05 height per ingot, and planning a gold color with a lighter highlight on top.

Most things get painted with cel shading for the toon look, while small elements like gems use flat colors with a glow instead, keeping the flat color palette down to around 20 colors since paints don't count against that limit. For the goblets, I'm planning three: an upright gold one with gems at front left, a tipped-over one spilling coins on the right, and a silver chalice with a ruby behind, each built via a lathe profile with a foot disc, stemmed knop, and flared bowl around 0.22 in height.

Working out the lathe coordinates for the upright gold goblet now...

I'll use around 10 segments for a slightly faceted, stylized look rather than smooth. For placing the goblet, I need to sink its foot into the mound at the right spot so it sits stably, maybe with a slight tilt for a natural resting look.

Now I'm adding ornamentation: a ring of small octahedral gems circling the bowl at a radius matching its taper, plus a jewel on the foot and a thin torus rim band oriented to match the goblet's tilted axis.

For the tipped-over goblet lying on the mound, I'm setting up a helper function that builds the lathe body, rim torus, and gems along a given axis, then positioning spilled coins streaming from its mouth as a fan of disc cylinders scattered along a spiral path across the mound surface.

Each coin needs semi-random orientation—mostly flat but with tilt variation and a few standing on edge—so I'm computing a numerical surface normal from the mound height function and aligning each coin's axis to it with some jitter, rather than relying on `setFromUnitVectors` since the guideline discourages that; I'll use the `aim(dir)` helper from the math module instead to get a proper quaternion.

I also need to account for the fact that the mounds are low-poly faceted hemispheres, so their actual surface sits slightly below the ideal smooth hemisphere due to polygon chord sag—roughly a few percent of the radius—which matters for how deep I sink each coin into the surface.

I'll settle on a 16x6 segment hemisphere with gentle vertical sag, sinking coins 0.01 along the normal for stability. For the coin pile itself, I'm planning around 520 coins with radius 0.045 and an exaggerated thickness of 0.011 for a stylized look, using a few color variations.

The coin area roughly matches the mound's surface area, so coverage should feel dense and layered rather than sparse. I'll add some vertical coin stacks of 5-7 coins at varying heights near the front as accent towers, plus a few coins leaning on edge for variety, keeping the coin faces as flat untextured color without rim detailing.

With flat shading, the top and side faces of each coin cylinder get different normals, which naturally creates a two-tone cel-shaded look without needing UV texturing. I'll vary the coin colors across a few gold tones plus some silver and copper, and could consider a simple embossed decal on the top face for detail.

For a handful of hero coins, I'll skip full texturing but add a small circle decal in front of each coin's face showing a simple emblem (concentric rings with a sun-spiral motif), tinted gold rather than grey, placed just in front of the coin face along its normal direction—building out seven of these via a helper function.

For gems scattered around, I'm considering using stretched octahedron geometry to get a faceted diamond-like shape rather than lathe-built cuts.

I realize full emissive strength would wash out facet shading, making gems look flat and bright instead of faceted. I'll dial emissive intensity down to around 0.45-0.5 so glowing gems keep their faceted shading while still reading as luminous, reserving full strength glow only for hero crystals.

Since glow only works on flat-colored standard materials (not painted ones), I need a different approach for regular gem facets — I'm considering a three-tone painted shading function based on normal direction that gives a faceted cel-shaded look with highlights, while reserving the glow-plus-flat-color treatment specifically for the larger magic crystals.

Now I'm planning the gem distribution across the mound — around 34 scattered gemstones mixing rubies, sapphires, emeralds, amethysts, topaz, and aquamarines, each getting cached paint functions by color.

I'm also designing two larger "hero" crystals, including a tall glowing hextech-style spire at the back-right built from a lathe profile with six-sided symmetry to give it that faceted crystal-tip look.

I'm clustering five smaller crystals tilting outward near that same mound area, glowing cyan and violet for a readable hextech aesthetic from above, then adding a few glowing gem pile pieces nestled in the chest heap, plus considering a draped pearl necklace swept along a path with beaded spheres.

Still working out necklace placement...

I'll shape an elongated pearl loop with a pendant draped over the mound front. Then I'm thinking about adding a few more scattered props beyond the brief's core items—maybe a gem ring, loose rubies, and a burlap coin sack with a cinched neck and spilling coins, though I should stay close to what was actually asked for: coins, gems, chest, crown, goblets.

Working out the sack's lathe profile now, placing it at the mound's left outer edge with a flared, belly-up shape and checking that the lip curves don't cross themselves geometrically.

For the finishing touches: a rope torus tied at the neck with small hanging tail rods, then nailing down a bold color palette for the chest—leaning toward a saturated dark teal-blue wood with gold trim bands, cyan hextech glow inside, and violet crystal accents for strong LoL-style contrast, with a gold crown topped by a ruby.

Writing plank paint logic...

Plank ends get lighter shading to show end-grain where the normal is near horizontal. Now I'm considering whether the body should just be a single box rather than built from separate wall pieces, since the interior needs to be visible from the top.

I'll make the body a solid box with a thin velvet "lining" plate placed near the top surface, leaving a narrow wood-colored rim visible around the edge, then place the heap hemisphere over the lining -- so it reads as an open box with contents rather than an empty shell.

Reworking the dimensions: body box with painted planks, a darker rim frame sitting above it with front/back and side bars, and a thin red lining plate inset at the interior top so the heap can fill up to about .46.

I'm generalizing the heap generation into a function that computes height from multiple hemisphere mounds combined with the floor mounds, taking the max across them so the chest heap dominates inside its footprint while the floor mounds stay lower outside it, with the velvet lining color applied underneath.

Since the chest is solid, I need to scatter floor coins and chest coins separately, excluding the chest's footprint rectangle from the floor scatter so coins don't end up embedded in the chest walls, adding a small margin near the front edge. I'll keep goblets and gems at explicit positions using the floor height function, then move on to the chest hardware colors — gold trim versus darker brass accents.

Working out corner bracket and strap positions...

Now I'm adding rivet details with small studs along the bands, plus designing a gold lock plate with a keyhole slot and a ruby accent.

I'm positioning the lock plate above the coin heap near the front, partially buried, then placing a small dark keyhole cylinder and slot just in front of the plate's surface, adjusting z-depths so it sits flush. Skipping chest feet since they're sunk into the mound.

For the base I'm adding a dark iron band near the bottom, slightly proud of the body. Then I'm working out the lid as an arched extrusion hinged at the back-top rim, computing the arch radius and hinge axis so the lid spans the body's depth and overhangs slightly for a proper fit.

Still shaping the arch...

When the lid is open at 105°, the underside becomes visible as a flat plank face, so I'll add a thin red velvet lining plate sitting just proud of that bottom surface, giving it a padded, studded look when viewed from inside.

I'm also figuring out the arch-shaped straps on the lid, building them as band outlines with an outer curve offset slightly from an inner curve matching the lid's own arch, positioned at both sides of the extrusion.

I should shift the center band aside to avoid the lock hasp, going with bands at x=±0.26 to match the body straps below for consistency. Then I need to place rivets as small spheres along each band's arch, mapped from the lid's curved coordinate frame onto the model surface.

Now I'm designing gold end plates for the lid sides at x=±0.43, thin extruded arch shapes slightly larger than the lid profile, each with a cabochon jewel centered on it. Lid parts all bind to the lid joint for the open pose, and I'm adding short gold hinge-knuckle cylinders along x near the hinge point.

I'm now working through the geometry of the lid opening at 105°, computing how the front edge and bulge rise and shift as the lid rotates about the hinge axis, tracking how the y and z coordinates transform under that rotation.

With the lid oriented, I'm now checking the full composition bounds—mound, crystals, bag, and open lid all fit within roughly x±1.25 and z from -0.95 to 1.4, centering the model on x=0.

I don't think a separate base disc is needed since the mound's flat-shaded hemisphere already has its base vertices sitting right at y=0. I'll scatter a few flat coins around the mound near the floor, keeping their sink within 2% of model height, and the hemisphere's triangle count (around 192 per mound, roughly 1.7k total across nine mounds) stays reasonable.

Now I'm defining the color palette for the coins -- gold, silver, and bronze variants with cel-shaded highlights and shadow tones, plus a reddish rose-gold and trim accents to give the coins visual variety.

For the velvet lining and lid underside, I'm working out a diamond-tufting pattern using the surface coordinates at the closed pose, computing a stitch grid from the horizontal plane positions to simulate quilted fabric texture.

Now I'm sketching SVG emblems for the chest's decorative elements, starting with a gold coin icon built from layered circles and a sunburst outline...

I'll skip the gem sparkle cards and scroll texture for now, but I'm planning glow elements -- crystals, a central crown gem, and glowing gems scattered through the chest's hoard interior.

I'll add a small column of rising sparks above the chest heap to give it a glinting treasure effect, then move on to writing the actual code with minimal, carefully-used imports and helper functions to reduce typos.

Writing TypeScript imports...

Now I'm setting up the builder structure, creating the root joint and a hinge joint for the lid.

Still writing helper types...

I also need the OutlinePoint type import, plus a vector helper, and a dome height function computing elevation from an ellipse-based bump shape, taking the max across multiple domes for terrain height at a point.

I'm estimating surface normals via numeric gradients, clamping heights at zero, then laying out a floor of dome bumps with specific positions and sizes around the scene, including one placed behind the chest/lid area to match the open-lid pose.

Checking the overall bounding box stays within ±1.45 on x. I need to make sure the coin scatter exclusion zone around the chest footprint properly accounts for the mound lobes that overlap it, since one lobe near x=0.8 spans into the chest's excluded region — that should keep coins from spawning inside the mesh, though I should double check the mound geometry itself doesn't clip through the chest walls.

For scattering coins across the mounds, I'm sampling random points within the bounding box of the dome union, accepting only points with positive height, then nudging each coin slightly along its surface normal with some random lift and tilt for natural variation — aiming for roughly 620 accepted placements. I'll keep the cel-shaded coin material consistent regardless of orientation.

Now I'm setting up cylinder geometries for each coin with low radial segments and flat shading for faceted edges, grouping them by color so I can merge each group into a single buffer geometry via matrix transforms for position, rotation, and scale. Then I pass each merged geometry into the paint/part system with flat normals recomputed after merging, guarding against null merges.

I'm wondering how the painting system handles UV baking for a merged geometry with 600+ coins and tens of thousands of triangles — whether it allocates texel patches per triangle in an atlas, and whether that could blow up memory or reduce texture density given the total coin surface area involved.

Given the density math works out wasteful for painted coins, I'm leaning toward skipping the paint bake for coins entirely and just using flat vertex colors with standard shading — small coins will still show lighting variation from facets, so the hard-surface look isn't lost, while avoiding the overhead of baking a huge merged mesh.

For the mound and domes, since most of that surface is hidden under the coins anyway, baking full painted texture there is mostly wasted area. I'm considering making the mound and domes flat-colored too, just dark gold, to save texel budget, though I need to check that any visible gaps between coins won't look flat and unfinished.

I'll keep painted textures reserved for the chest, goblets, crown, bag, and gems, estimating roughly 8 m² of painted surface overall which gives a reasonable texel density. Small hardware details like rivets and studs can use flat colors too, while the larger plates stay cel-shaded.

Now I'm working out the chest wood paint function, planning plank boundaries with dark line seams and noise-based grain variation along the wood direction.

Shadows get folded through the cel paint conversion, skipping nail details on plank ends. For the chest body, top and bottom faces are covered by the rim so I don't need extra plank treatment there, while lid planks need an arch angle computed from the lid's position.

I'm defining the lid wood paint and gold trim colors, and considering adding engraved rivet rows or a decorative filigree texture to the gold bands for extra ornamentation on the chest front.

Working out the band and panel positioning...

Actually that's too cluttered—I'll simplify by placing flourish decals flanking a central lock plate, sized small enough to fit the gap, with gold texture on transparent background and strokes thick enough to render clearly at the chosen resolution.

Now I'm defining a basis helper that builds front/side vectors orthogonal to a given axis, then uses them to compute points and radial directions around a ring for placing decorative elements consistently along the crown's curved surface.

Now I'm planning spire placement around the crown — tall pointed spires at the front, sides, and back (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°), with smaller fleur shapes filling the gaps between, while making sure the big front gem stays visible rather than hidden behind a spire.

I'm working out the geometry for each spire base: computing its position and tangent direction along the band, then extruding an outline scaled by height depending on whether it's a tall or short spire. Writing the spire outline shape...

The edges narrow convexly toward the tip without crossing, so smoothing level 1 should be safe here. I'm also planning a small pearl sphere at each spire tip and considering whether to add gems at the spire bases or just place them along the band instead.

For the band gems, I'm spacing them every 45 degrees with alternating colors, with the largest gem centered at the front. Each gem is a lathed shape oriented radially so its table faces outward and the tip embeds into the band wall, with size scaled relative to the girdle radius.

Defining the gem outline as a closed polygon with points for the tip, girdle, crown ring, and axis top to form a faceted brilliant-cut profile, using 8 segments for the lathe. For the large front gem, I'm sizing it with a shallow embed depth and considering a flat red glow color, though noting painted gems can't actually glow.

For the facet appearance on glow gems, I'm leaning toward flat shading with reduced emissive intensity (~0.55-0.6) so lighting differences stay visible, while painted gems use a separate paint function. I'm writing a gem helper function that takes position, axis, size, color, and optional glow strength, branching between glow and painted rendering paths, plus planning bead rows along the band edges using small gold spheres.

Now I'm working out the band's decorative engraving—thinking through a chevron/zigzag stripe pattern using a sine or modulo function on the lathe angle to darken specific zones, creating a filigree-like ridged effect around the ring's band.

I'm also setting the crown's tilt direction with a normalized axis vector so it leans naturally toward the viewer, and tallying up the total crown height between the band and spire sections to get the final exaggerated proportions.

Now I'm placing the two goblets on the mound: an upright gold one near the front-left adjusted to sit at the correct lobe height, and a silver chalice further right positioned relative to the crystal cluster and crown location, computing its mound height offset to settle it realistically into the surface.

I'm also working out the third goblet, tipped over near the front center with coins spilling toward the camera, figuring out its axis orientation from foot to mouth and solving for the foot's height on the mound surface.

Since it's lying on its side, I need to position it so both the bowl rim and foot edge rest convincingly on the surface, with the axis sloping slightly rather than perfectly horizontal to match how the coin heap tilts downward at the front.

Small sinking at the foot is fine since coins will hide it. I'm planning the spilled coins streaming from the mouth position, generating a batch along the forward path with jitter and lift, using a coin-placement helper that samples the surface height for each one.

For the vertical stacks, I'm computing base positions sunk slightly into the surface with per-coin jitter and yaw, keeping the stack axis straight vertical rather than normal-aligned so they stand upright on sloped ground. I'm placing six stacks of varying heights near the ingots, plus one toppled stack sliding sideways.

Now I'm adding hero detail to each stack's top coin with a circular emblem decal facing upward, and working out how a few leaning coins propped against the pile should orient along a horizontal axis toward the viewer.

For the standing coins I'm solving the vertical offset needed so the coin's edge just touches the surface given its tilt angle, then placing five larger, exaggerated coins near the front of the pile using that formula.

Now I'm mapping out six spots for additional small details, carefully checking coordinates against the existing crown, goblets, chalice, ingots, bag, and crystals so nothing overlaps, and working out where to position a necklace loop and its height against the dome's curve.

Next I'm placing coin stacks around the scene, calculating positions near the chalice and a mound, verifying each stack's height against the dome's curvature to keep them sitting naturally on the surface.

I'm checking the ingots and bag placement don't overlap with the coin stacks, keeping proper spacing, then arranging the standing hero coins and goblets so their radii stay clear of each other.

Placing the hero coin leaning against the chest front, facing outward. Now scattering gems: 30 random gems checked against reserved circular zones around the crown, goblets, chalice, ingots, bag, and necklace, with orientation jitter and varied sizes/colors, plus 5 special larger glowing gems mixed in for sparkle accents.

For the coin scatter, I want to avoid coins clipping badly into reserved object footprints while still letting them pile naturally around bases, so I'll reuse the reserved-zone check but with a smaller effective radius for coins since they're flatter and can tuck closer.

Now I'm working out crystal placement for a cluster near the mound's dome, computing the surface height at that spot so the crystal bases sit correctly, then figuring out the hex prism geometry for each crystal shape.

I'm using a six-sided lathe profile with a pointed tip, flat-shaded for a low-poly crystalline look, and considering how to add a moderate glow so facets stay visible rather than washing out into one flat color -- possibly adding a darker base tone to suggest rock at the bottom of each crystal.

Now I'm laying out the crystal cluster itself—six crystals of varying lengths and radii, each tilted at different angles outward from a shared base region, with their positions offset slightly from the cluster center to create a natural radiating arrangement.

I want a second, smaller violet crystal cluster placed off to one side near the bag, plus a scattering of tiny glowing octahedra sparks floating above the chest heap—seven of them in white-gold and cyan tones with a stretched vertical shape for extra sparkle.

For the star-shaped glints, I'm deciding between textured planes or card primitives anchored to a frame, oriented to face the viewer with a double-sided star texture so they read clearly from the front.

I'll apply glow to the card meshes, using a diamond-cross star SVG shape in gold and cyan variants, placing eight such stars across the crown tip, goblet rims, gem tops, and the chest heap for a bright accent. Then I pose the lid by rotating it -105 degrees around the X axis, making sure this happens after all lid parts are built and before anything that depends on the lid's final orientation.

The stars and chest heap are independent of the lid pose though, so now I'm building the treasure pile on the chest: defining a dome shape for the main mound plus smaller domes nearby, scattering around 90 coins and some glowing gems across its surface within a bounded x/z region. I'm constructing the dome itself as a flattened hemisphere mesh in a warm gold-brown color, scaled per-dome to control its width and height, with flat shading for a faceted look.

For non-uniform scaling I'm relying on the normal matrix to keep lighting correct despite the squashed geometry, and since the hemisphere's base is open and hidden, that's not an issue visually. I'm picking a darker gold tone for the mound itself so it contrasts against brighter coins piled on top, then designing gold ingots using a four-sided cylinder with cel-shaded lighting so the top face reads bright and the sides shade darker, possibly adding a thinner lighter plate on top for extra detail.

For the ingot top surface I'm using a normal-based paint function that checks if the surface points upward to apply a highlight color versus the base gold on the sides, letting the key light naturally brighten the lit top face. I'm also considering adding a small stamped decal, like a dark rectangular mark oriented along the ingot's length using an up-vector parameter. Now I'm moving on to designing the burlap bag texture with a woven, mottled color pattern using two tan shades for visual texture.

For the bag, I'm figuring out how to add a stitched emblem decal to the front using a decal function that takes a target part, texture, position, direction, and size, placing a coin-like symbol (ring and star design) roughly at the bag's front-facing surface position.

I'm also planning spilled coins around the bag mouth, positioning five coins in a tilted circular arrangement, and scattering about fourteen more coins on the floor around the mound's edge.

Now I'm placing those edge coins outside the mound radius with randomized yaw and slight tilt. I'll skip adding a scepter, but I'm considering a small gold ring with a gem, oriented upright and resting somewhere on the mound.

Still adjusting coin and ring placement...

Writing gem helper function...

Still defining paint caching logic...

Defining the facet lighting logic...

Still defining the goblet outline types and lathe geometry...

I'm confirming that nested paints correctly inherit the surface coordinates from the outer resolve call, so cel shading reads the right light threshold. Now I'm positioning the rim torus geometry around the ring, orienting it along the radial direction at the foot point.

I'm placing a gold trim torus for the foot ring bead, then adding a gem ring around the bowl base—six gems positioned radially outward at a slight embed depth, sized relative to the knop radius. I'm also considering filling the goblet's interior with a heaped dome of coins for visual richness.

For the coin heap, I'm sizing a hemisphere dome and positioning it along the bowl's interior axis, checking that its radius matches the bowl's inner taper at that height and that its peak stays just above the rim without overflowing.

I'm topping the coin pile with a small gem, around .03k in size, glowing like a gem at the apex. For color schemes I'm planning gold with emerald gems for one goblet, silver with ruby and violet glow for the chalice, and gold with sapphire for the tipped goblet — the tipped one will have its bowl opening toward the spill direction with coins placed near the mouth. The lathe axis orientation revolves the profile along the given direction from the foot point toward the bowl, which checks out. Now I'm moving on to designing the silver chalice's profile, which needs a wider, shorter bowl with a knop detail.

Now I'm checking overall proportions: reusing the same outline with a scaled variation, adding velvet cushion paint for the crown, and verifying the model's height comes to about 1.0 meter with a footprint around 2.9 by 2.4 meters — larger than a typical prop but still reasonable for a dragon's hoard. I'm confirming the lowest points of each piece sit right at y=0 so everything rests properly on the ground.

Now I'm setting up core constants for the chest geometry — center position, width, depth, height, rim height, and hinge location — then defining a helper function that generates arch-shaped point arrays for the lid's curved profile.

Writing arch point generator...

Then I plan the band shell outline by offsetting the arch outward for thickness.

With top v=.21, the lid depth of .56 slightly overhangs the body's .54, so the lid extends from z=-0.78 to -0.22. I place the hinge at the back edge, giving HINGE = [0, .39, -0.78].

Now I'm setting up the lid wood extrusion with its arch outline and bevel, attached to the lid bone, then adding the flat lining piece underneath to represent the lid's underside.

I'm also adding the gold trim bands on the lid at symmetric x-positions, plus gold end plates sized slightly larger than the lid arch to cap the edges near the lid's width boundary.

Now I'm placing small gem jewels centered on those end plates, oriented outward, and planning the front hasp as a shield-shaped tab overlapping both the lid's front wall and the body front where the lock sits.
